It helped establish him as more than an artist who delivered memorable verses on other people’s songs. Bad Since ’97 (2022) With Bad Since ’97 , BNXN became more confident in his identity and sound. Released in August 2022, the seven-track EP featured Wizkid , Wande Coal and Olamide , three established artists whose presence added to its appeal. “Many Ways,” “Kenkele” and “Modupe” gave listeners different sides of his artistry, while the title track reinforced the self-assurance that runs through the project. It arrived in a year when his contribution to Pheelz ‘s “Finesse” had further raised his profile, making the EP an important follow-up to his breakthrough. Although critics differed on the consistency of its production, the project demonstrated his growing ability to hold his own alongside established names. The Game Needs Us (2026) Four years after Bad Since ’97 , BNXN teamed up with producer Sarz for The Game Needs Us , a five-track EP released in May 2026. The collaboration is particularly interesting because it allows the singer’s melodies and songwriting to meet Sarz’s distinctive production. From “Rum & Soda” to “Emotional High” and “Already,” the project balances romantic vulnerability with the sort of rhythms that work equally well on headphones and dance floors. Its strongest commercial statement came with “Back Outside,” which topped Spotify Nigeria’s daily songs chart. More impressively, all five tracks entered the platform’s Nigerian top 15 in the same period. That suggested that listeners engaged with the project beyond a single hit. Still in Charge (2026) BNXN followed that collaborative outing with Still in Charge , a six-track EP released on 1 October 2026. Featuring Asake on “Eja Meja” and FOLA on “Shamaya,” the project moves between self-assurance, romance and carefree enjoyment. “Online” addresses conversations about his absence from social media, while “Deliberate Work” offers a more pointed look at his experiences in the industry. “If You Like” closes the project on a lighter note, leaving listeners with a glimpse of an artist comfortable with his position. The EP also debuted on Apple Music’s Nigerian albums chart. Across these four projects, BNXN has demonstrated that an artist doesn’t necessarily need to release an album every year to remain relevant. Each EP provides a focused glimpse into his development, collaborating with some of the industry’s most recognisable names while continuing to experiment with his sound. While his albums offer a broader view of his artistry, his EPs consistently give listeners compelling reasons to pay attention. The industry often prioritises quantity; BNXN makes a strong quality case as well. The post BNXN Has The Best EP Projects in Afrobeats appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Hong Kong club hope David Silva can be their hero – but just for one day
item.description: Former Manchester City player is coming out of retirement at 40 to play one match for ambitious Supreme Sha Tin Hong Kong, China (as is the official football name), has long tried to follow the advice of Han Solo in Return of the Jedi: keeping their distance from China while trying not to look like they are keeping their distance. It is all about maintaining an independent football association and the trappings and privilege that come with it. There was some talk a few years ago about getting a Hong Kong team in the Chinese Super League, when the spending was in full flow, and although that did not happen the local Premier League has belatedly got in on the act – kind of. This glittering city is not known as a football hotbed but has a long history in the sport that started when it was a British colony and has continued since it became a special administrative region of China in 1997. George Best, Peter Shilton, Arie Haan, Bobby Moore, Diego Forlán, Nicky Butt, René van de Kerkhof, Tony Morley, Gordon McQueen and Craig Foster have played in the territory and soon David Silva will too. Continue reading...

item.title: Stories Behind the Frame: The Memories Nigerians Are Unearthing for NB@80
item.description: Some photographs only reveal their true weight with time. A childhood birthday, a family Christmas, a traditional marriage or an old gathering can seem ordinary when the picture is taken, only to become more meaningful years later as the people, circumstances and memories around them change. That is what is beginning to emerge from Nigerian Breweries’ Together, Every Moment, as Nigerians revisit old photographs and videos and share the stories behind moments that once seemed routine. Across the entries received so far are memories shaped by family, growth, humour, loss and unexpected connections to brands that have been part of Nigerian life for decades. For content creator Virtuous, one of those memories came from a family gathering during her childhood. In the photographs she shared, drinks from Nigerian Breweries appear on the table, an ordinary detail at the time but one that would later take on a different meaning. Years after those pictures were taken, she went on to work with Amstel Malta , creating an unlikely link between a childhood memory and her adult career. “If you told the girl in the first and second slides that she would grow up to work with the brands she held in her hands as a child, she absolutely would have believed you. I always knew please ,” she joked. For Stella Ezenwata , the memory is tied to her traditional marriage in January 2017, an occasion she can now laugh about even though it felt far less amusing at the time. The marriage list specifically requested Star, Heineken or Gulder, but when a different drink was brought instead, the family insisted it be returned. Another item requested for the Umuada could not be found, leaving the couple to offer money in its place. “Honestly, the stress no be here,” Stella recalled. Nine years later, what was once a stressful part of the day has become one of the stories she remembers most clearly. Ralph ’s entry reaches further back, to his sixth birthday shortly after his family moved into a new home. The photograph shows children gathered indoors, some caught mid-dance, with bottles of Maltina visible in the foreground. What stayed with him was the excitement of marking his birthday in the new house, surrounded by family. It is the kind of childhood moment that can feel small at the time but grows in meaning with distance. For @ anna4manuel , that passage of time changed the meaning of her memory in a more painful way. She shared a Christmas video of her family dressed in red, gathered around a dining table and preparing for the festivities, with bottles of Maltina among them. Nothing about the footage immediately suggests why the moment has stayed with her so strongly. It looks like a familiar family Christmas, one of those occasions that can easily be taken for granted while everyone is still together. I always knew please ,” she joked. For Stella Ezenwata , the memory is tied to her traditional marriage in January 2017, an occasion she can now laugh about even though it felt far less amusing at the time. The marriage list specifically requested Star, Heineken or Gulder, but when a different drink was brought instead, the family insisted it be returned. Another item requested for the Umuada could not be found, leaving the couple to offer money in its place. “Honestly, the stress no be here,” Stella recalled. Nine years later, what was once a stressful part of the day has become one of the stories she remembers most clearly. Ralph ’s entry reaches further back, to his sixth birthday shortly after his family moved into a new home. The photograph shows children gathered indoors, some caught mid-dance, with bottles of Maltina visible in the foreground. What stayed with him was the excitement of marking his birthday in the new house, surrounded by family. It is the kind of childhood moment that can feel small at the time but grows in meaning with distance. For @ anna4manuel , that passage of time changed the meaning of her memory in a more painful way. She shared a Christmas video of her family dressed in red, gathered around a dining table and preparing for the festivities, with bottles of Maltina among them. Nothing about the footage immediately suggests why the moment has stayed with her so strongly. It looks like a familiar family Christmas, one of those occasions that can easily be taken for granted while everyone is still together. Her caption gives the video an entirely different meaning. “I didn’t know it would be my last Christmas with my father,” she wrote. What was once simply a record of a family celebration is now a reminder of a moment she can never recreate. The entries reflect how differently memories can age. Some become funnier with time, some take on new meaning as life changes, while others become more precious because of what came after them. The photographs may capture a single moment, but the stories around them often reveal much more. One of the most striking examples came not from a photograph, but from a comment shared during the anniversary conversation. Instagram user @dr_deraaa revealed that her grandfather, who turns 105 this month, spent 35 years working at Nigerian Breweries in Aba before retiring in 1985. Growing up, she said, the family often heard stories about his years with the company, memories he still cherishes and speaks about today. If the dates in her account are accurate, his career would have begun around 1950, only a few years after Nigerian Breweries was established. That connection offers a different perspective on the company’s 80-year history. For his family, the story is not only about the occasions on which Nigerian Breweries products appeared, but also about the working life of a man whose career became part of that history. It is this broader idea that sits at the heart of the National Story Collection. As part of Nigerian Breweries’ 80th anniversary campaign, Together, Every Moment, Nigerians are being invited to share photographs and videos that capture how the company, its brands and its wider presence have intersected with their lives over the years. Eighty selected entries will each receive ₦1 million. Actress and comedian Kiekie , entertainer Real Warri Pikin and Nollywood actor Odunlade Adekola are among those who have joined the anniversary conversation and encouraged Nigerians to revisit their own memories. But the strongest stories emerging so far are the ones that feel least manufactured: a birthday in a new home, a traditional marriage that did not go quite to plan, a childhood photograph that later came full circle, a final Christmas with a loved one, and a 105-year-old man still telling stories from a career that began more than seven decades ago. Together, they show why the most interesting part of a photograph is often not what appears in the frame, but everything the frame comes to mean afterwards. To participate, share a photo or video featuring a Nigerian Breweries product and tell the story behind the memory. item.title: A Seat for You and Your Bestie: Brutal Fruit Brings Women Together at The Pink Table Milan
item.description: Brutal Fruit’s The Pink Table brought Pan-African competition winners, their best friends and guests from across Africa together in Italy, making friendship the occasion for an international escape. Some experiences are made better by the person standing beside you. A beautiful view becomes the place you both promise to return to. A song becomes your song. Before you have found the words, she already understands. And when something feels almost too good to be real, one look at your best friend is enough: can you believe we are here? Much of the joy of female friendship lives in that shorthand. There is comfort in being known, in having someone who understands your sense of humour and shares the memories behind it. Taking that friendship somewhere new adds another chapter to a story already in progress. It can also make room for other people to enter it. Brutal Fruit’s The Pink Table Milan began with that feeling and an invitation to let the circle grow. From September 25th, competition winners and their best friends from across Africa and Brazil came together against the backdrop of Milan Fashion Week and Lake Como. The invitation had a simple starting point: bring your bestie. The consumer winners earned their places through retailer competitions, with each invited to bring her bestie. The details shaped the experience from the outset. A prize for one woman became an occasion for two, giving each pair someone familiar to share the excitement with as they stepped into a wider gathering. Born in South Africa, The Pink Table has travelled from home to Paris and now Milan with female friendships at its centre. The trip brought African women into an international setting alongside guests from elsewhere in the world, with time to find common ground through food, fashion and music. Female friendships have always been at the heart of The Pink Table and in Milan, bringing a bestie meant arriving with someone who knew you, while joining women from other countries and backgrounds offered the chance to get to know someone new. The South African spritzer brought them together through experiences designed to give connection room to materialize. A table is a good place to start and the welcome meal at Nonna’s captured that spirit. Generous Italian food, conversation and laughter brought warmth to a new setting. Sharing a table gave guests time to settle in and form camaraderie, creating an easy introduction to the women around them. The food belonged to Italy, but the pleasure of getting to know someone over a meal felt familiar. Fashion gave the conversation another kind of spark. At Barbara Rizzi’s show, where Brutal Fruit was the official drinks partner, winners, besties and creators experienced the work of a female-led Italian luxury label known for its craftsmanship and bold contemporary design. The details shaped the experience from the outset. Born in South Africa, The Pink Table has travelled from home to Paris and now Milan with female friendships at its centre. The South African spritzer brought them together through experiences designed to give connection room to materialize. A table is a good place to start and the welcome meal at Nonna’s captured that spirit. Generous Italian food, conversation and laughter brought warmth to a new setting. Sharing a table gave guests time to settle in and form camaraderie, creating an easy introduction to the women around them. The food belonged to Italy, but the pleasure of getting to know someone over a meal felt familiar. Fashion gave the conversation another kind of spark. At Barbara Rizzi’s show, where Brutal Fruit was the official drinks partner, winners, besties and creators experienced the work of a female-led Italian luxury label known for its craftsmanship and bold contemporary design. There were looks to admire and impressions to exchange, giving guests a shared experience to talk about beyond their own friendship pairs. Milan offered other points of discovery too. At Museo Bagatti Valsecchi, Renaissance art and antiques added another dimension to the city’s creativity. Alongside the fashion, these encounters gave women with different backgrounds something to discover together. Milan’s appeal was also its ability to create those openings: a new setting, a shared interest and a reason to start a conversation. Music made that common ground especially clear. A 19-member performance team led by pianist Julian Cohen brought songs including Coldplay’s “Viva la Vida”, “Bella Ciao” and Whitney Houston’s “I Wanna Dance With Somebody” into the experience. For guests who had not all arrived knowing one another, a familiar song offered something immediately recognizable to enjoy together. Brutal Fruit’s L’Orange Rossa , which was inspired by the Italian Riveria, added a flavour of the destination to the occasion. But the detail that held these different experiences together was the company; the best friend you came with, and the women you knew you had a reason to get to know. At Lake Como, the wider circle came together at The Pink Table itself. Around 75 guests from across the world including South African actress Siphesihle Ndaba , content creator and influencer Sni Mhlongo gathered at Villa Regina Teodolinda in Laglio, where sprawling gardens opened to private access to the water providing a romantic and intimate backdrop. Hosted by Italian actress Marina Valdemoro Maino, the occasion brought food, music and conversation into one setting. For all its beauty, the villa offered something simple; it gave women somewhere to gather and time to spend together. Besties could sit beside one another while becoming part of a larger table. The comfort of an existing friendship and the possibility of a new connection belonged in the same space. At The Pink Table Milan, female friendships were both the reason to gather and the starting point for new connections. Across countries and backgrounds, Brutal Fruit gave women the space to discover what they shared. Bringing a bestie was the beginning of the invitation. Making room for a wider circle was its promise. Because while the destination was Milan, the real currency of the trip was connection. item.title: Have any footballers ended their career with more own goals than goals? | The Knowledge
item.description: Plus: the earliest trophyless seasons, scoring off one’s backside (part II) and the origins of ‘shithousery’ Mail us with all of your questions and answers “How many professional players have ended their senior careers with more own goals than goals for their own team?” wonders Peter Clark. In the past we’ve looked at the players with the most own goals , but we haven’t looked at those who ended their professional career in debit. “Southampton cult hero Francis Benali scored only one ‘positive’ goal in his career and was legendary for banging in goal-of-the-month contenders at his own end, most notably a bullet header against Oldham in the 1993-94 season ,” writes Daz Pearce. We could only find a couple of OGs for Benali, the other being against Manchester United in 1999-2000 . But we were unable to find a comprehensive Southampton database, so there’s a chance we’ve missed some beauties. Continue reading...

item.title: On this day in space! Oct. 13, 1773: Astronomer Charles Messier discovers the Whirlpool Galaxy before we ever knew it was a galaxy
item.description: null On Oct. 13, 1773, a French astronomer named Charles Messier discovered the " Whirlpool Galaxy , " also known as Messier 51, or M51. Charles Messier was scanning the sky for objects that could confuse comet hunters when he catalogued the galaxy as M51. However, Messier wasn't able to see the spiral structure, and he didn't identify it as a galaxy. Seventy-two years later, another astronomer named William Parsons saw the whirlpool shape, but he thought it was a spiral nebula. Eventually, Edwin Hubble found out that M51 and other features like it were actually galaxies. Spiral galaxy M51 (NGC 5194), The Whirlpool Galaxy, displays its long arms which consist of stars and gas laced with dust arranged in long lanes, in this view from the Hubble Space Telescope. The smaller galaxy to the right is NGC 5195, which is actually more distant than M51, and not next door. (Image credit: NASA/ESA/S. Beckwith/Hubble Heritage Team/STScI/AURA) Why it mattered The Whirlpool Galaxy is located about 31 million light-years from Earth and just might be the textbook case of a spiral galaxy . But in 1773, it was just one of 51 (at the time of its discovery) of "comet-like 'objects to avoid'" in the night sky. The Whirlpool Galaxy's designation as M51 marks it as the 51st non-comet object catalogued by Messier, who was the chief astronomer of the Marine Observatory in Paris dedicated to studying comets. According to a NASA account , Messier stumbled across his first non-comet object, M1 (also known as the Crab Nebula ), while studying a comet in 1758. The objects looked like fuzzy blobs like comets, but didn't move like a comet. By 1773, at the time he first spotted M51, he had catalogued over four dozen such objects to help prevent astronomers from mistaking them for comets . The Whirlpool Galaxy appears as a dazzling spiral in images by the Hubble Space Telescope, and has a magnitude of 8.4 on the brightness scale used by astronomers. That means it can be observed through a small telescope ("most easily during May," NASA says ) in the constellation Venatici (the Hunting Dogs) in the northern sky, just below the handle of the Big Dipper star pattern . Scientists suspsect the Whirpool Galaxy gets is striking spiral shape from a close interaction with its neighbor galaxy NGC 5195 , which may have passed through M51's main disk about 500 million years ago, scientists with NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope have said. "This gravitational tug of war may also have triggered an increased level of star formation in M51," they added in a statement . "The companion galaxy's pull would be inducing extra starbirth by compressing gas, jump-starting the process by which stars form." Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: See the original Galileo shuttle from 'Star Trek' in its new home at the Original Series Set Tour in New York
item.description: null Nostalgia is a hell of a thing, especially when it comes to sci-fi. For "Star Trek" fans wanting to mark the franchise's 60th anniversary this year, a geeky pilgrimage to upstate New York should be on the cards. Why? Because alongside the splendid autumnal colors, they can steer over to Ticonderoga to behold the newly installed Galileo shuttlecraft. After a complete two-year restoration project in 2012 headed up by superfan and collector Adam Schneider, this iconic fictional spacecraft, seen by millions in seven episodes over three seasons of "Star Trek: The Original Series," was recently relocated from its former home at the Johnson Space Center Museum in Houston, Texas. It's now on permanent loan to James Cawley and his Star Trek Original Series Set Tour in historic downtown Ticonderoga, New York, where it joins a family of painstakingly detailed sets based on the official "Star Trek" blueprints. The Galileo's cozy new home with a cool starfield backdrop! (Image credit: James Cawley/Star Trek Tour) 'Galileo is still the property of Space Center, and it was on display there since 2013," Schneider tells Space. "It went to USS Intrepid for the 50th anniversary of 'Star Trek,' displayed under the Enterprise Space Shuttle. You had the Enterprise with Enterprise's little shuttle Galileo adjacent, which was an extraordinary picture. It went back to Space Center, but it takes up an enormous amount of room, and they took it off display after 8 years." It seemed a shame to have the shuttle out of sight, so Schneider got to work finding a new home for the shuttle. "Since I was on the board, I tried to figure out a place where it could be aimed", recounts Schneider. "The Star Trek Tour made the most sense, so I worked with Space Center to relocate it, and it arrived a couple of years ago." Hoping to give the restored relic its own private docking bay due to its enormity, faithful fans raised hundreds of thousands of dollars via a Kickstarter campaign led by Brian Mix and David Harvey, and built a beautiful building addition for Galileo to be safely ensconced in. (Image credit: Star Trek Tour) "My wife Leslie and I had been tending over the Galileo for a number of years, and it's now successfully displayed there in New York for all to see," Schneider adds. "It's an extraordinary thing to see person if you have not. It's not the size of a chair, it’s the size of a bus. It looks gorgeous in its new space, and if you’re a space aficionado or Star Trek aficionado, that’s even more reason to get involved with this thing." Opening weekend for the general public at Star Trek Tours to see the newest member of the museum was Sept. 18-20, 2026, and the Galileo was the star attraction. Branded Trekonderoga Weekend, the unveiling ceremony was attended by Assemblymen Dan Stec and Dan Simpson, and 'Trek' luminaries George Takei, Jonathan Frakes, and Brent Spiner. It's now on permanent loan to James Cawley and his Star Trek Original Series Set Tour in historic downtown Ticonderoga, New York, where it joins a family of painstakingly detailed sets based on the official "Star Trek" blueprints. The Galileo's cozy new home with a cool starfield backdrop! (Image credit: James Cawley/Star Trek Tour) 'Galileo is still the property of Space Center, and it was on display there since 2013," Schneider tells Space. "It went to USS Intrepid for the 50th anniversary of 'Star Trek,' displayed under the Enterprise Space Shuttle. You had the Enterprise with Enterprise's little shuttle Galileo adjacent, which was an extraordinary picture. It went back to Space Center, but it takes up an enormous amount of room, and they took it off display after 8 years." It seemed a shame to have the shuttle out of sight, so Schneider got to work finding a new home for the shuttle. "Since I was on the board, I tried to figure out a place where it could be aimed", recounts Schneider. "The Star Trek Tour made the most sense, so I worked with Space Center to relocate it, and it arrived a couple of years ago." Hoping to give the restored relic its own private docking bay due to its enormity, faithful fans raised hundreds of thousands of dollars via a Kickstarter campaign led by Brian Mix and David Harvey, and built a beautiful building addition for Galileo to be safely ensconced in. (Image credit: Star Trek Tour) "My wife Leslie and I had been tending over the Galileo for a number of years, and it's now successfully displayed there in New York for all to see," Schneider adds. "It's an extraordinary thing to see person if you have not. It's not the size of a chair, it’s the size of a bus. It looks gorgeous in its new space, and if you’re a space aficionado or Star Trek aficionado, that’s even more reason to get involved with this thing." Opening weekend for the general public at Star Trek Tours to see the newest member of the museum was Sept. 18-20, 2026, and the Galileo was the star attraction. Branded Trekonderoga Weekend, the unveiling ceremony was attended by Assemblymen Dan Stec and Dan Simpson, and 'Trek' luminaries George Takei, Jonathan Frakes, and Brent Spiner. Does anyone think the Galileo shuttlecraft might have been the inspiration for Tesla's Cybertruck?! (Image credit: Adam Schneider/Star Trek Tour) "We're certainly thrilled that we were able to work with Adam and NASA to get it here permanently," Cawley tells Space. "Then to get it on display properly and share it with all the fans and make sure that it's on exhibit for many years to come. We’re just outside of the village of Lake George, so we’re part of the greater Lake George tourism region. "You've seen it on television, and now you’re the caretaker of it. What an honor to be able to do that. It’s the simplicity of the Galileo that makes it so unique. It's Matt Jefferies' whole design ethic for the original series. Less is more. It catches your eye in a specific way. It has a blocky-type silhouette and actually it really complements the Enterprise because you really see the shape difference. Everything has that mid-century modern aesthetic. It's just timeless." Adam and Leslie Schneider pose beside the gleaming Galileo shuttle (Image credit: Adam Schneider/Star Trek Tour) For Cawley, being custodian and host of the screen-used Galileo is like a dream. This 23-foot-long mock-up was part of the USS Enterprise's basic design and was rescued from demolition some 14 years ago when Schneider purchased it at a 2012 memorabilia auction for $61,000. "We had a great rousing opening weekend with it, and business has been very steady into October with people asking about it. It's going to be a big cornerstone to the tour. I think people are becoming aware that it’s here and they’re making a pilgrimage to come because of it." For more prices, hours, and more information on the Star Trek Original Series Set Tour in Ticonderoga, New York, visit them at https://startrektour.com or call 518-503-5497. You can also see the Galileo in action in Star Trek: The Original Series on Paramount+. item.title: 'We basically did Top Gun in space': 'Star Trek Starfleet Academy' warps back into action in March 2027 for sophomore year in the final frontier
item.description:
Tariq is the Editor-in-Chief of Space.com based out of our New York City office and joined the team in 2001, first as an intern and staff writer, and later as an editor. He covers human spaceflight, exploration and space science, as well as skywatching and entertainment. He became Space.com's Managing Editor in 2009 and Editor-in-Chief in 2019. In October 2022, Tariq received the Harry Kolcum Award for excellence in space reporting from the National Space Club Florida Committee. In June 2025, the National Space Society awarded him the Space Pioneer Award for Excellence in Mass Media at the International Space Development Conference in Orlando, Florida.

Hailing from Stockton, California (where he attended the same high school as NASA astronaut Jose Hernandez), Tariq studied print journalism and astronomy at the University of Southern California in Los Angeles, earning a bachelor's degree in journalism in 1999 along with a minor in astronomy. He then served as a staff reporter for The Los Angeles Times covering education and city beats in La Habra and Fullerton in Orange County for the Our Times sections.

In 2000, Tariq became the city reporter for the Huntington Beach Independent, a weekly publication of the Los Angeles Times, covering local politics and events, crime, business and environmental issues. He left the Los Angeles Times in 2001 to study science journalism at New York University, where he earned a master's degree in 2002 from NYU's Science and Environmental Reporting Program (now the Science, Health and Environmental Reporting Program) under the direction of space reporter William Burrows.

Tariq first joined Space.com as an intern in September 2001 while also serving as a research assistant for nutrition writer Gary Taubes and writing freelance projects, where his work appeared in The Scientist and Laboratory Equipment Magazine. He became a full-time reporter covering spaceflight in 2004, with this first launch being NASA's STS-114 Return to Flight mission in July 2005.

Tariq is also an Eagle Scout (yes, he has the Space Exploration merit badge) and went to Space Camp four times as a kid and a fifth time as an adult. When not writing about space, you can find Tariq watching the latest Star Trek TV series, sci-fi movies and reading about hippos, his favorite animal. You can find Tariq at Space.com and as the co-host to the This Week In Space podcast with space historian Rod Pyle on the TWiT network. To see his latest project, you can follow Tariq on Twitter @tariqjmalik.

To see his latest project, you can follow Tariq on Twitter @tariqjmalik.

NEW YORK — Set your phasers to back-to-school, space fans. Star Trek is going back to Starfleet Academy for season 2, and we finally have a release date. The sophomore season of " Star Trek: Starfleet Academy " will warp back to the small screen in March 2027 when the limited series returns for its final season on Paramount+ . The series, which follows a class of cadets balancing Starfleet classes, space adventures (and yes, some love) in the 32nd century, will return with its full cast and even add new faces, showrunners announced at a panel at New York Comic Con 2026 on Saturday (Oct. 10). "Season one is about letting go of who you were in the past to start again at Starfleet Academy," executive producer and co-showrunner Noga Landau said in the Star Trek panel. "Season two is about thinking that you knew who you were, only to realize that as you grow older, your life is going to go in directions you didn't expect, and you're going to have to shift your perception of yourself. So it's really about sophomore year, right?" Paramount+ Essential (ads): $5.99 /mo Paramount+ with SHOWTIME (no ads): $11.99 /mo Star Trek: Starfleet Academy will be available to watch on Paramount+. You can also watch almost every other Star Trek show and movie on there, too, while you wait. View Deal Holly Hunter returns as academy chancellor Nahla Ake , a long-lived half-Lanthanite, who will have to face a familiar face in her estranged father, Nyk Ake, portrayed by Bill Nighy (Living, About Time) in season two. "He plays my full lanthanide father, who has basically, if he wants, can achieve immortality," Hunter said, dropping a big preview about her character in season two. "He plays my dad, and I play me ... and my twin, my twin sister. Very fun." Also joining this year's Starfleet Academy class is Rosemarie DeWitt (Untamed, The Staircase) as Laytha Sadal, the First Lady of Betazed (and mother of Academy cadet Tarima). Bill Nighy on Starfleet Academy Season 2 as Nyk Ake, father of the chancellor Nahla Ake. Michael Gibson/Paramount+ Rosemarie DeWitt (right) on Star Trek: Starfleet Academy as the First Lady of Betazed. Michael Gibson/Paramount+ "We have had such a blast," Hunter said of working with the entire cast of Starfleet Academy. "It was a tremendous honor and learning experience for me to do the show for two seasons, and I just really am excited about the second season because there's so much more intimacy that we just comfortably felt with each other over those 10 episodes." In season one, Starfleet Academy brought back Trek's favorite Emergency Medical Hologram, The Doctor (Robert Picardo), then gave the 800-year-old Star Trek: Voyager physician a daughter in the photonic Sam (Kerrice Brooks) and a Klingon medical student, Jay-Den Kraag (Karim Diané), to train. We basically did Top Gun in space ..." showrunner Alex Kurtzman "His future existence is forever changed. Nothing will ever be the same for the character," Picardo said in the panel. "The shock of that, and how that changed the character, [...] informs all of season two. My primary relationships are now with my daughter and of course with Jay-Den, as I'm mentoring him as a future physician, and we have some terrific scenes together as well." Executive producer and co-showrunner Alex Kurtzman promised more space action in season two of Starfleet Academy and showed an exclusive teaser clip of Academy cadets Caleb (Sandro Rosta), Genesis (Bella Shepard) and Sam as they race to recover data from a crashed spaceship on their first away mission. But the best, Kurtzman said, is yet to come when the show's cadets meet up with Nova Squadron, the elite flight team at Starfleet Academy. "The Nova Squadron episode is amazing on a lot of different levels," Kurtzman said. "We basically did Top Gun in space. "What's available to us now technologically allowed us to go to a place that I don't think we've ever gone to on television before. Certainly not in Star Trek." Star Trek: Starfleet Academy will return to TV in March 2027 on the Paramount+ streaming platform. item.title: Earth's poles shifted surprisingly fast during the age of dinosaurs, ancient sea levels reveal
item.description: The location of Earth's geographic poles has changed several times over the past 320 million years in a process known as true polar wander, according to measurements of ancient flooding brought about by sea level changes resulting from our planet's crust shifting relative to Earth's spin axis. Such a shift can affect climate, both on local scales and globally, as regions that were by the poles find themselves moving down to lower latitudes and vice versa. This can then affect atmospheric circulation patterns, which affect climate across the world. The changes would have affected the environments in which life developed and evolved, from the age of the dinosaurs through to some of our oldest primate ancestors. True polar wander is not the same as a change in the rotational axis of the Earth . Currently, Earth spins at an angle of 23.4 degrees relative to the plane of its orbit around the sun, and this rotational axis can vary periodically over tens of thousands of years as a result of the Milankovitch cycles caused by the gravitational pull of the sun and planets. True polar wander is different. Here, the angle of Earth's spin axis does not change relative to its orbital plane. Instead, Earth's crust and mantle shift relative to that rotational axis. This is because Earth is not perfectly spherical. Instead, it is oblate, with Earth's rotation causing the equator to bulge out and the poles to slightly flatten. Because Earth is not spherical, it has multiple axes of inertia, the largest one being aligned with the rotational axis. These axes need to be balanced to prevent Earth's rotation from becoming chaotic. However, plate tectonics and indeed the Milankovitch cycles can upset that balance of mass, for example by causing more continental crust to congregate in one hemisphere than another. To rebalance things, Earth's crust and mantle must become decoupled from our planet's core, which stays aligned with the rotational axis. In physical terms, if there is more continental crust in one hemisphere, the crust and mantle might rotate in that direction relative to the rotational axis and the Earth's core in order to balance itself. This sees the geographical locations of the poles change, hence the name 'true polar wander'. Currently, true polar wander takes place at a rate of 10 centimeters (4 inches) per year, but figuring out when and how fast true polar wander has occurred in the past is not without its difficulties, not least since plate tectonics can mask and even mimic the signal of true polar wander. Previous studies relied on paleomagnetism, the study of residual magnetic traces in ancient rocks, since the orientation of those magnetic traces would have varied depending upon where that rock was located relative to Earth's magnetic field . item.dc:creator: Keith Cooper
item.content:encoded: The location of Earth's geographic poles has changed several times over the past 320 million years in a process known as true polar wander, according to measurements of ancient flooding brought about by sea level changes resulting from our planet's crust shifting relative to Earth's spin axis. Such a shift can affect climate, both on local scales and globally, as regions that were by the poles find themselves moving down to lower latitudes and vice versa. This can then affect atmospheric circulation patterns, which affect climate across the world. The changes would have affected the environments in which life developed and evolved, from the age of the dinosaurs through to some of our oldest primate ancestors. True polar wander is not the same as a change in the rotational axis of the Earth . Currently, Earth spins at an angle of 23.4 degrees relative to the plane of its orbit around the sun, and this rotational axis can vary periodically over tens of thousands of years as a result of the Milankovitch cycles caused by the gravitational pull of the sun and planets. True polar wander is different. Here, the angle of Earth's spin axis does not change relative to its orbital plane. Instead, Earth's crust and mantle shift relative to that rotational axis. This is because Earth is not perfectly spherical. Instead, it is oblate, with Earth's rotation causing the equator to bulge out and the poles to slightly flatten. Because Earth is not spherical, it has multiple axes of inertia, the largest one being aligned with the rotational axis. These axes need to be balanced to prevent Earth's rotation from becoming chaotic. However, plate tectonics and indeed the Milankovitch cycles can upset that balance of mass, for example by causing more continental crust to congregate in one hemisphere than another. To rebalance things, Earth's crust and mantle must become decoupled from our planet's core, which stays aligned with the rotational axis. In physical terms, if there is more continental crust in one hemisphere, the crust and mantle might rotate in that direction relative to the rotational axis and the Earth's core in order to balance itself. This sees the geographical locations of the poles change, hence the name 'true polar wander'. Currently, true polar wander takes place at a rate of 10 centimeters (4 inches) per year, but figuring out when and how fast true polar wander has occurred in the past is not without its difficulties, not least since plate tectonics can mask and even mimic the signal of true polar wander. Previous studies relied on paleomagnetism, the study of residual magnetic traces in ancient rocks, since the orientation of those magnetic traces would have varied depending upon where that rock was located relative to Earth's magnetic field . Alas, it's not a terribly accurate means of measuring true polar wander and scientists arrived at substantially different conclusions using this technique. Nevertheless, based on paleomagnetism, scientists had concluded that true polar wander had been negligible, or slow to proceed, in the distant past. However, new results from researchers at the Centre for Planetary Habitability at the University of Oslo in Norway, led by Mathew Domeier, have shown this not to be the case. Domeier's team looked through the geological record to track how sea level has changed across millions of years. True polar wander would bring about an identifiable pattern in sea-level changes as the oceans reacted in response to changes in the mass distribution of the planet. The sea level changes would be equal but opposite between hemispheres — sea level rises on one side of one hemisphere would be matched by rises on the other side of the opposite hemisphere, creating a 'quadrupolar' effect. By using statistical modeling on maps of sea level changes across intervals of 10 million years, Domeier's team identified four periods of true polar wander: in the early Jurassic period 190—200 million years ago, the late Jurassic — early Cretaceous period 140—150 million years ago, during the mid-Cretaceous 90—100 million years ago and from the Oligocene period 30 million years ago through to the Miocene 20 million years ago. The results show that, contrary to established opinion, true polar wander can happen in bursts that are relatively fast on geological timescales, with the results showing that during the episodes of true polar wander the Earth's surface shifted by as much as 0.6 degrees per million years relative to the spin axis. This is slow by human standards, but fairly fast on geological timescales, certainly quicker than plate tectonics. Domeier's team were also able to rule out a suspected case of true polar wander around 300 million years ago when the last great supercontinent, Pangea, migrated northwards. It turns out that Pangea's movements were entirely due to plate tectonics. The findings were published on Oct. 1 in the journal Science .

item.title: SpaceX rocket launch creates incredible 'space jellyfish' visible throughout US East Coast (photos)
item.description: null Rockets are launching to space on a near-daily basis these days, but short of livestreaming a liftoff from the comfort of your Wi-Fi router, relatively few spectators are in the right place and time to see one with their own eyes. That wasn't the case Tuesday morning (Oct. 13), when SpaceX launched the CRS-35 mission for NASA . A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Pad 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida at 6:35 a.m. EDT (1035 GMT), carrying a cargo variant of SpaceX's Dragon spacecraft on the company's 35th commercial resupply mission to the International Space Station (ISS). Following the northward path of the space station's orbit at the time, the rocket flew a trajectory along the United States' East Coast. Falcon 9's expanding engine plume grew substantially wider than the rocket itself as it climbed in altitude into thinner, less dense air, and was illuminated by the early dawn light, making the sight visible to millions. "You can imagine my surprise when I opened my back door to let the dogs out this morning," Ellen Alence told Space.com. She snapped a pic of the rocket from her farm Colbert, Georgia. "Many of you are talking about the 'space jellyfish' following this morning's launch from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida," NASA's Kennedy Space Center wrote in a post on X . The post explains the "jellyfish" phenomenon that is sometimes visible during dawn and dusk launches, and included additional photos of the launch. Ellen Alence This morning’s SpaceX rocket launch, as seen from a farm in Colbert, Georgia. Ellen Alence "A jellyfish happens near sunrise or sunset when the exhaust plume from the rocket becomes brightly illuminated, creating a glowing shape resembling a jellyfish," the post said. October 13, 2026 Further up the coast, Richard Mack Wilson-Leigh spotted the flight from Durham, North Carolina. His view of the rocket came just seconds before the vehicle's stage separation, which was followed immediately by the rocket's main booster performing an engine burn to right its trajectory for landing back at the Cape. Following the northward path of the space station's orbit at the time, the rocket flew a trajectory along the United States' East Coast. Falcon 9's expanding engine plume grew substantially wider than the rocket itself as it climbed in altitude into thinner, less dense air, and was illuminated by the early dawn light, making the sight visible to millions. "You can imagine my surprise when I opened my back door to let the dogs out this morning," Ellen Alence told Space.com. She snapped a pic of the rocket from her farm Colbert, Georgia. "Many of you are talking about the 'space jellyfish' following this morning's launch from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida," NASA's Kennedy Space Center wrote in a post on X . The post explains the "jellyfish" phenomenon that is sometimes visible during dawn and dusk launches, and included additional photos of the launch. Ellen Alence This morning’s SpaceX rocket launch, as seen from a farm in Colbert, Georgia. October 13, 2026 Further up the coast, Richard Mack Wilson-Leigh spotted the flight from Durham, North Carolina. His view of the rocket came just seconds before the vehicle's stage separation, which was followed immediately by the rocket's main booster performing an engine burn to right its trajectory for landing back at the Cape. Wilson-Leigh said that part caught him off guard more than the initial site of the rocket. "I thought it blew up at first," he jokingly told Space.com. "At first, I thought it was a comet ," Wilson-Leigh said. "My mind jumped between two thoughts: that is just beautiful beyond belief, and it is the end of the world.” SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket soars above the skies of Durham, North Carolina. (Image credit: Space.com / Richard Mack Wilson-Leigh) That stage separation came about 2.5 minutes after liftoff, and put on a dazzling display for those awake to see it this morning. As Falcon 9's booster began the journey to its landing zone, the rocket's second stage continued onward to orbit with Dragon and the capsule's 6,300 pounds (2,860 kilograms) of cargo for the ISS. The spacecraft will spend roughly two days catching up to the ISS, where a recent personnel rotation swapped the astronauts of SpaceX's Crew-12 mission with those of Crew-13. The latter arrived aboard the orbital laboratory Oct. 1, which was followed several days later by the return of Crew-12 to Earth on Oct. 8. Falcon 9 launches the CRS-35 mission to the @Space_Station https://t.co/QiHIqlDLTH October 13, 2026 (Image credit: SpaceX) The Dragon carrying the contents of CRS-35's manifest will arrive at the station Thursday morning (Oct. 15), and will autonomously dock to the space-facing port of the Harmony module at around 11 a.m. EDT (1500 GMT). Coverage of the arrival here at Space.com beginning at 9:15 a.m. EDT (1315 GMT).

item.title: 2 spacecraft in orbit and 8 more coming soon: Varda has big plans for in-space manufacturing
item.description: null Reentry and orbital-manufacturing provider Varda Space Industries is operating two spacecraft in orbit right now, with another expected to launch "in the coming days" and seven more next year. The Los Angeles-area startup, which bills itself as one of just two companies that can currently do commercial reentry from space, successfully launched its latest two refrigerator-sized spacecraft aboard SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare mission on Oct. 1. "It's humanity's first time launching multiple commercial reentry vehicles simultaneously," Varda CEO Will Bruey told Space.com on Tuesday (Oct. 7) of the Transporter-18 launch. The payloads on the Transporter-18 Varda craft ranged from pharmaceuticals to demo navigation systems to exterior thermal-protection materials. The company bills its spacecraft as mini-factories, which can host the orbital production of valuable goods such as pharmaceuticals and then bring them safely down to Earth. Another Varda vehicle is scheduled to follow them into space later this month. Assuming the third spacecraft launches nominally, all three will come down before Christmas in the Koonibba Test Range in the South Australian Outback, through coordination with Varda's long-time space-mission service provider, Southern Launch. And things are scheduled to ramp up quickly: Varda aims to fly seven more missions in 2027: two in Quarter 1 (Q1), two in Q2 and three in Q3 (the latter three being all on the same rocket). "As we scale up, we care about our ability to fly and fly regularly," Bruey said, emphasizing that the company is now treating its missions less as one-offs and more as a series. "It is, first and foremost, taking that unique [spacecraft] technology and moving into a fleet mentality, rather than a space mission mentality." One of Varda's reentry capsules is seen shortly after its touchdown in the Australian Outback. (Image credit: Varda Space/Rocket Lab) Like any startup finding its footing, Varda's challenges in the coming months will be scaling safely and efficiently. But the company says it is well-capitalized to do so, and has a big hiring campaign underway. It also has been spending money on slight upgrades and improvements to its vehicles, as well as mission operations and other infrastructure to run several missions at the same time, with more funds having just arrived. In September, Varda announced it had raised $251 million in "Series D" investment funding and will be hiring 100 people by the end of 2027, boosting its current 286-employee base by more than a third. Most of the employees work out of El Segundo, California, with a few in sales offices in Washington, D.C. and Huntsville, Alabama (where U.S. Space Command is gradually moving , along with some defense contractors, from Colorado Springs). In the further future, Bruey said, the goal is to fly Varda vehicles into space daily, using a "standardized product" that would be put together on an assembly line. "It's humanity's first time launching multiple commercial reentry vehicles simultaneously," Varda CEO Will Bruey told Space.com on Tuesday (Oct. 7) of the Transporter-18 launch. The payloads on the Transporter-18 Varda craft ranged from pharmaceuticals to demo navigation systems to exterior thermal-protection materials. The company bills its spacecraft as mini-factories, which can host the orbital production of valuable goods such as pharmaceuticals and then bring them safely down to Earth. Another Varda vehicle is scheduled to follow them into space later this month. Assuming the third spacecraft launches nominally, all three will come down before Christmas in the Koonibba Test Range in the South Australian Outback, through coordination with Varda's long-time space-mission service provider, Southern Launch. And things are scheduled to ramp up quickly: Varda aims to fly seven more missions in 2027: two in Quarter 1 (Q1), two in Q2 and three in Q3 (the latter three being all on the same rocket). "As we scale up, we care about our ability to fly and fly regularly," Bruey said, emphasizing that the company is now treating its missions less as one-offs and more as a series. "It is, first and foremost, taking that unique [spacecraft] technology and moving into a fleet mentality, rather than a space mission mentality." One of Varda's reentry capsules is seen shortly after its touchdown in the Australian Outback. (Image credit: Varda Space/Rocket Lab) Like any startup finding its footing, Varda's challenges in the coming months will be scaling safely and efficiently. But the company says it is well-capitalized to do so, and has a big hiring campaign underway. It also has been spending money on slight upgrades and improvements to its vehicles, as well as mission operations and other infrastructure to run several missions at the same time, with more funds having just arrived. In September, Varda announced it had raised $251 million in "Series D" investment funding and will be hiring 100 people by the end of 2027, boosting its current 286-employee base by more than a third. Most of the employees work out of El Segundo, California, with a few in sales offices in Washington, D.C. and Huntsville, Alabama (where U.S. Space Command is gradually moving , along with some defense contractors, from Colorado Springs). In the further future, Bruey said, the goal is to fly Varda vehicles into space daily, using a "standardized product" that would be put together on an assembly line. But to get to that point, like other companies in the industry, Varda will need to get through an anticipated rocket shortage beginning in about 2029. SpaceX is by far the most active launcher these days, and it has been the dominant provider for companies like Varda via its Transporter and Bandwagon rideshare programs. But SpaceX is readying to retire its Falcon 9 rocket as it transitions more resources into Starship , the fully reusable megarocket the company sees as its workhorse of the future. Media reports suggest that SpaceX is pretty much out of capacity for Falcon 9 rockets flying through the end of service in 2028 or 2029, although slots are still available through third-party bookers. There are a slew of newer rockets under production (such as Blue Origin's New Glenn and Relativity Space's Terran R ), though they are far less mature and in some cases, even unflown. This is creating uncertainty about how much capacity there will be in the industry in the short term, but Varda said it is planning well ahead for that moment — and so too are its customers. "We're stacked with launches from now through that 2029 time frame," Bruey said. The company's current generation of vehicles is "launch-agnostic," although the next generation is aiming to be even more so to nab opportunities from small rockets up to Starship. The company said that, as long as Varda and its customers have access to microgravity , the shipping methodology — much like shipping on Earth — should not matter, and Varda aims to make the experience that seamless for its customers. But in the meantime, the company says it will fly as much as possible and (like everyone else) do what it can to secure slots on launching rockets after Falcon 9 retires.

item.title: Dettol Nigeria: Storytelling Wraps Up Challenge with 30 Winners
item.description: Dettol Nigeria has concluded its “12 Hour Protective Shield” storytelling challenge, recognizing 30 Nigerians for sharing personal stories about their experiences with Dettol Original Antibacterial Bar Soap. The Dettol Original 12hrs Protection Challenge ran from 13 July to 31 August 2026, and invited Nigerians to share personal Dettol stories ranging from childhood memories to family and personal hygiene routines. After the challenge closed, 30 winners were selected and rewarded with cash prizes for their entries. The challenge was part of the wider campaign for Dettol Original Soap, built around its 12-hour protective shield against 99.9% of illness-causing germs. Under the campaign idea, “ 12 Hours, Protection That Moves With You, ” Dettol highlighted the importance of consistent hygiene as people move through their daily activities. Beyond the digital campaign, Dettol brought the experience directly to consumers through in market activations across multiple states in Nigeria, combining product education and demonstrations with handwashing stations and consumer engagement. Commenting on the campaign, Boma Harrison , Marketing Director, Reckitt West Africa , said, “We were particularly pleased to give Nigerians the opportunity to share their personal Dettol stories and hear what protection means to them and their families. The stories shared through the challenge reflect the place Dettol has held in Nigerian households over the years, while reinforcing the importance of hygiene in everyday life. ” The campaign brought together digital storytelling, consumer engagement and on-ground experiences to reinforce Dettol Original’s role in everyday hygiene routines, while giving Nigerians an opportunity to share the personal experiences that have shaped their connection with the brand. item.title: Fashion Innovation Africa to Convene 300+ Stakeholders at Inaugural Conference in Lagos on October 22
item.description: Fashion Innovation Africa (FIA) 2026 will bring together more than 300 stakeholders from across fashion, finance, technology and government to examine the structures, investments and partnerships needed to build a stronger and globally competitive African fashion industry. Scheduled for Thursday, October 22, 2026, at Landmark Event Centre, Victoria Island, Lagos, the inaugural business conference is themed “From the Atelier to the Economy: The Architecture Behind African Fashion”. Endorsed by the Lagos State Government, FIA 2026 will focus on the systems and capabilities required to translate Africa’s creative talent into sustainable businesses, jobs and wider economic opportunities. The conference will convene successful fashion founders and business leaders alongside representatives from government, regulatory agencies, financial institutions, technology companies, logistics providers and other stakeholders across the fashion value chain. By bringing these groups together, FIA aims to strengthen connections between the creative, commercial and institutional players whose collaboration is essential to the industry’s growth. The full-day programme will feature a Government Keynote, fireside chats with leading founders, three panel discussions and concurrent masterclasses. Discussions will address critical industry issues, including access to growth capital, local manufacturing, supply chain resilience, quality standards, technology, trade frameworks and access to international markets. Uche Ajene , Convener of Fashion Innovation Africa, said the conference draws inspiration from the growth of Nigeria’s music and film industries, which have built stronger commercial structures and expanded their global reach over time. “There was a time when Nigerian music and Nollywood had immense talent but were still building the structures needed to support their growth and global reach. Today, both have made significant strides in taking Nigerian creativity to the world,” she said. “African fashion has similar potential, but realising it requires more than talent and visibility. We need stronger systems for financing, production, distribution, standards and market access. FIA is bringing the key players together to help build that architecture and position African fashion for sustainable growth and global competitiveness.” Beyond the conference programme, FIA 2026 will provide opportunities for businesses and industry stakeholders to showcase solutions, exchange ideas, build strategic partnerships and explore commercial opportunities across the fashion value chain. Fashion Innovation Africa is an initiative focused on strengthening Africa’s fashion ecosystem by connecting the people, businesses and institutions that shape its growth. Through industry convenings, strategic collaborations and opportunities for knowledge exchange, FIA seeks to advance the infrastructure, investment and market access needed to build a more connected, commercially sustainable and

item.title: 'Space Gal' Emily Calandrelli launches into the Marvel Universe this week on Disney Jr.'s 'Iron Man' series (exclusive)
item.description: null "The Space Gal" is blasting off onto her next adventure to promote STEM education with out-of-this-world content. Science communicator and citizen astronaut Emily Calandrelli, better known to millions of social media followers as "The Space Gal," is bringing her real-world spaceflight experience to the Marvel universe . Calandrelli is lending her voice to an upcoming episode of Disney Jr.'s animated series, "Marvel's Iron Man and his Awesome Friends." She is stepping into the role of a character called Astronaut Amy in the episode "The Iron Friends in Space," offering another opportunity for Calandrelli to share her enthusiasm for space with younger audiences. Astronaut Amy meets characters on "Marvel's Iron Man and his Awesome Friends." (Image credit: Disney) Calandrelli is an engineer, author and television host whose career has focused on making complex scientific concepts engaging and accessible. Growing from her online presence as @TheSpaceGal , Calandrelli has produced numerous educational videos, books and television appearances, including a role on the Netflix "Bill Nye the Science Guy" revival series, "Bill Nye Saves the World." In a preview clip provided exclusively to Space.com by Disney, Calandrelli's character is welcomed by Tony Stark, Riri Williams, Amadeus Cho and Vision as they explore a moon-themed museum display. The exhibit features a holographic model of the moon and other space-themed artifacts, providing a backdrop for Astronaut Amy to share information about space and lunar exploration. The show follows younger versions of Stark and others from Marvel's familiar superhero roster, as they navigate conflicts that are scaled down from the franchise's world-ending blockbuster emergencies to more age-appropriate problem-solving and teamwork-building storylines. Calandrelli's cameo puts her alongside characters already rich in their storylines with backgrounds in science and technology, like Stark and Williams, known by their alter egos Iron Man and Ironheart, both of whose superhero identities revolve around the mastery of sophisticated technology and engineering. And while Astronaut Amy and her super co-stars live in Marvel's fictional universe, Calandrelli's inclusion in the episode creates the opportunity to introduce some real-life scientific concepts. Her appearance also comes as Disney prepares to expand the animated series to include a larger ensemble. Beginning next summer, the show will evolve into "Marvel's Avengers: Mightiest Friends", and bring additional characters into the fold, including Captain America, Hulk, Black Panther, Black Widow and Thor, according to Disney. item.content:encoded: null "The Space Gal" is blasting off onto her next adventure to promote STEM education with out-of-this-world content. Science communicator and citizen astronaut Emily Calandrelli, better known to millions of social media followers as "The Space Gal," is bringing her real-world spaceflight experience to the Marvel universe . Calandrelli is lending her voice to an upcoming episode of Disney Jr.'s animated series, "Marvel's Iron Man and his Awesome Friends." She is stepping into the role of a character called Astronaut Amy in the episode "The Iron Friends in Space," offering another opportunity for Calandrelli to share her enthusiasm for space with younger audiences. Astronaut Amy meets characters on "Marvel's Iron Man and his Awesome Friends." (Image credit: Disney) Calandrelli is an engineer, author and television host whose career has focused on making complex scientific concepts engaging and accessible. Growing from her online presence as @TheSpaceGal , Calandrelli has produced numerous educational videos, books and television appearances, including a role on the Netflix "Bill Nye the Science Guy" revival series, "Bill Nye Saves the World." In a preview clip provided exclusively to Space.com by Disney, Calandrelli's character is welcomed by Tony Stark, Riri Williams, Amadeus Cho and Vision as they explore a moon-themed museum display. The exhibit features a holographic model of the moon and other space-themed artifacts, providing a backdrop for Astronaut Amy to share information about space and lunar exploration. The show follows younger versions of Stark and others from Marvel's familiar superhero roster, as they navigate conflicts that are scaled down from the franchise's world-ending blockbuster emergencies to more age-appropriate problem-solving and teamwork-building storylines. Calandrelli's cameo puts her alongside characters already rich in their storylines with backgrounds in science and technology, like Stark and Williams, known by their alter egos Iron Man and Ironheart, both of whose superhero identities revolve around the mastery of sophisticated technology and engineering. And while Astronaut Amy and her super co-stars live in Marvel's fictional universe, Calandrelli's inclusion in the episode creates the opportunity to introduce some real-life scientific concepts. Her appearance also comes as Disney prepares to expand the animated series to include a larger ensemble. Beginning next summer, the show will evolve into "Marvel's Avengers: Mightiest Friends", and bring additional characters into the fold, including Captain America, Hulk, Black Panther, Black Widow and Thor, according to Disney. For Calandrelli, the role represents another extension of a career dedicated to making space exploration relatable and exciting for the next generation. In November 2024, Calandrelli became the 100th woman to reach space when she launched aboard Blue Origin 's New Shepard rocket on the company's NS-28 suborbital mission. The flight carried her above the Kármán line , the internationally recognized boundary of space, and gave her several minutes of weightlessness before the capsule and its crew returned to Earth . Calandrelli isn't the first real-life astronaut to lend her voice to the Marvel universe. Former NASA astronaut and the first Black woman in space Mae Jemison guest-starred in Disney's "Marvel's Moon Girl and Devil Dinosaur" in March 2023. Jemison voiced a fictional app called Skipster, created by the show's young superhero and scientific prodigy, Lunella Lafayette. Another space traveler, citizen astronaut Kellie Gerardi, also just announced over the weekend (Oct. 12) her cast credit in the upcoming movie "Hexed", from Disney's Animation Studios. Viewers can catch the upcoming episode of "Marvel's Iron Man and his Awesome Friends," titled, "The Iron Friends in Space," during its Disney Jr. premiere on Oct. 14 or streaming on Disney+ beginning Oct. 28. item.title: Companies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling back
item.description: Rapid AI adoption left workers cleaning up a flood of errors and low-quality work Employers around the globe are grappling with the fallout from rushing to adopt fast-changing artificial intelligence tools. Meta has scaled back plans to axe staff and use more AI agents after the company found employees were spending more and more time cleaning up technical and security errors, Reuters reported . And after thinning its workforce, especially middle managers , in a 2023 efficiency push, the company is expanding its managerial ranks again, LinkedIn posts from workers show. Continue reading...

item.title: Desperados and Young Jonn Create a Cross-Cultural Anthem For Living In The Moment With ‘Let It Go’
item.description: From the infectious rhythms of Latin music to the unmistakable pulse of Afrobeats, Desperados and Young Jonn are bringing two cultures together on “Let It Go, ” a new track inspired by living in the moment. Some moments are best enjoyed without overthinking them: a spontaneous night out, an unexpected link-up with friends, or the song that gets everyone moving. Capturing this spirit of freedom and self-expression, Desperados has teamed up with award-winning Afrobeats producer, songwriter and artist Young Jonn for “Let It Go.” Produced by Yung Willis , the Grammy-nominated music producer whose production credits span some of the biggest names in African music. Having worked with notable artistes including Falz, Wizkid, Kizz Daniel, Davido, Niniola, BNXN, Zlatan, Patoranking and Ice Prince , Yung Willis brings his production expertise to the collaboration, helping shape a sound that connects global influences with the energy of Afrobeats. Rooted in the brand’s identity and association with self-expression, Desperados continues to find meaningful ways to connect with the younger audience through music, culture and premium experiences. With “Let It Go”, the brand is using music as a touchpoint between its Latin roots and the energy of Nigerian culture. At the heart of the collaboration is “ Guao Guao ,” the reggaeton track Desperados created in partnership with Venezuelan artist Micro TDH and Colombian producer Ovy On The Drums. Built around a sample of this unique record, Let It Go brings a Latin-inspired sound into Young Jonn’s style, creating an Afrobeats song that reflects Nigeria’s vibrant music and nightlife culture. “Let It Go” is more than a fusion of two sounds. It is an expression of the Desperados vibe, where music becomes a way to encourage people to loosen up and enjoy moments that make life memorable. By connecting the global influence of Latin music with Afrobeats, the brand reinforces its place through music, culture, and self-expression. Young Jonn’ s ability to reinterpret global influences through a distinctive Nigerian style makes him a fitting partner for this expression. Rather than recreating the original, he gave the sound a fresh identity, shaped by the rhythm and movement of Nigerian music. Whether it’s the rhythm that takes over the dance floor, an ordinary link-up that turns into a memorable experience, the song captures the freedom of letting go and being fully in the moment. For Desperados, the brand’s involvement gives the song a cultural expression, connecting its identity to a sound that brings people together, encourages movement and creates room for memories. From recreating dance moves to sharing interpretations through lifestyle content, fans can join the “Let It Go” vibe beyond simply listening. item.title: Mark Your Calendars! Ecclesia Hills Church Announces 6th Ecclesia Word Conference, “Freedom in Christ”
item.description: Ecclesia Hills Church is pleased to announce the sixth edition of the Ecclesia Word Conference, themed “Freedom in Christ.” The conference will take place from Friday, 6th November to Sunday, 8th November 2026, at The Hall, 16 Musa Yar’adua Street, Victoria Island . The Ecclesia Word Conference has grown into a gathering where believers are taught, equipped, and stirred to live out the fullness of their faith. Last year’s edition explored the theme Custodian of Holy Oracles . This year’s edition turns to a question at the heart of the Gospel: What is freedom in Christ, and how can the Ecclesia arrive there? “This conference is crucial to bringing believers to the accuracy of freedom,” said Pastor Moses Ida-Michaels , Pastor of Ecclesia Hills Church. “Many people carry the name of Christ yet remain bound by religion, fear, habits, financial pressure, and generational patterns. This gathering is about seeing freedom clearly and walking in it. Together, we will hack the principles that bring true liberty to life,” he concluded. Conference Focus Across three days, sessions will address freedom in every area of life, including: Free a Generation: El-Shakar Freedom from Religion: Jabar Mckellar Freedom from Mammon: Chris Delvan Freedom in Illumination: Eva Dan Yusuf Freed Bloodlines, Cycles, Enchantments: Edem Julius-Cudjoe Freedom from Sinful Addictions / Fear of Consequence: Chris Delvan Free to Serve God’s Purpose: Chris Delvan Freedom in Innovation / Innovative Liberty: Moses Ida-Michaels (Host Pastor) Liberty Ideology: Edem Julius-Cudjoe Worship will be led by Hill Music and Moses Akoh , creating an atmosphere for encounter, response, and transformation. item.title: More Than Just a Glass of Milk: A Dietitian’s Perspective on Why Milk Matters
item.description: If you grew up in Nigeria in the 90s or early 2000s, chances are you didn’t learn about milk from a science class. You learnt about it from television. Back then, adverts were part of our childhood. We didn’t reach for a remote every time the commercials came on. We sang the jingles, quoted the catchphrases and years later, many of us can still remember them word for word. For me, one advert stands above the rest. It followed a young Kanu Nwankwo as he dribbled a football through the dusty streets of Owerri on an errand for his mother. He left home with nothing but a football at his feet, dribbling all the way to the market. Just as a tin of milk slipped from the market woman’s hands, he flicked it back into the air with effortless skill. She smiled and said, “Papilo, I know say one day you go make us proud.” As children, we believed her. Not because we understood marketing, but because those adverts made us believe that greatness could begin anywhere. They told us that a boy from Owerri, Nigeria could become one of Africa’s greatest footballers. They told us that ordinary children with big dreams could grow into extraordinary adults. And somewhere between that advert and my mum pouring Milk into my breakfast cereal every morning before school, I came to believe two things. The first was that milk helped build strong bones and teeth. The second was that maybe, just maybe, I could become whoever I dreamed of becoming. Years later, after becoming a dietitian, I realised that my childhood understanding wasn’t wrong, it was simply incomplete. Today, conversations about milk have become surprisingly complicated. Social media is filled with conflicting opinions. Some people insist milk is only for children. Others believe it causes weight gain. Some assume all milk is the same, while others believe dairy milk and non- dairy offer identical nutrition. As nutrition professionals, we know that the truth is rarely found in headlines or viral videos. It is found in evidence. So, let’s separate what we know about milk from what we only think we know.
